column2: [Vaishampayana] Hear, tiger among kings, the great and supreme marvel that happened, lord, when the great horse sacrifice was over.
When the best of brahmins, kinsmen, relatives and friends, and the wretched, blind and poor had been satisfied, best of the Bharatas,
while the great gift was proclaimed in all directions, O Bharata, and showers of flowers fell on the head of the king of dharma,
a mongoose with golden side came out of a hole, blameless one, and uttered a cry like a thunderbolt, lord of the people.
Having uttered that cry once, frightening beasts and birds, the great bold hole-dweller spoke in a human voice:
This sacrifice, kings, is not equal to a measure of barley-meal of the generous gleaner living at Kurukshetra.
Hearing those words of the mongoose, lord of the people, all those best of brahmins were struck with great amazement.
Then, meeting the mongoose, those twice-born asked: "Where do you come from, to this sacrifice, a fine gathering?
The whole tradition, unbroken, has been performed by priests who know the rules; as the tradition and justice say, and what was to be done has been done.
Those worthy of honour have been honoured here by rule with the eye of scripture; the fire has been offered into, purified by mantras; what was to be given has been given without envy.
The best of brahmins here are satisfied with gifts of many kinds, kshatriyas with good battle, the grandfathers with shraddhas,
the vaishyas satisfied with protection, fair women with desires, shudras with compassion, common people with the remains of gifts,
the kinsmen and relatives with our king's purity, the gods with oblations, holy rites and those who took refuge with protection.
What is true here, tell us, true to your word, brahmins asking as they wish about the twice-born, as heard and as seen.
Your word is credible, you are wise and bear a divine form; having met the brahmins, you should speak truly."
Thus asked by those twice-born, the mongoose laughed and said: "This word was not spoken falsely by me, nor out of pride, brahmins.
What I said and you heard: this sacrifice, kings, is not equal to a measure of barley-meal of the generous gleaner living at Kurukshetra."

So I must tell you this, best of brahmins; listen with undistracted mind as I tell, chiefs of brahmins.
mahabharata:14:92.21	The marvel, supreme, experienced and seen by me, how the gleaner living at Kurukshetra lived,
mahabharata:14:92.22	by which a brahmin with his wife, son and daughter-in-law reached heaven, and how half my body was turned to gold.
In the dharma-field of Kurukshetra, crowded with many knowers of dharma, there was long ago a brahmin gleaner, a pigeon-liver.
With his wife, son and daughter-in-law he stood in austerity, the fourth being the daughter-in-law; the old man was righteous and self-controlled.
At the sixth time the brahmin of good vows ate with them; sometimes at the sixth time there was no food for him, and the best of brahmins ate then at another time.
When a terrible famine came, brahmins, that one who lived like a pigeon had no store; learn it: the herbs were spent and he became without goods.
When time after time came and no food was found, all of them, seized by hunger, remained so.
Gleaning in the bright fortnight, with the sun burning at midday, tormented by heat and hunger, the brahmin in austerity found no gleanings with his household.
Seized by hunger likewise, having touched water by rule, the best of brahmins, barely alive, passed that time.
Then, when the sixth time passed, he obtained a prastha of barley, and those ascetics made it into barley-meal.
Greeting that guest and asking after his welfare, those of pure mind, self-controlled, with faith and restraint,
free of envy, free of anger, good, free of malice, having given up pride, conquerors of anger, knowers of dharma, best of brahmins,
having told one another their celibacy and clan, brought the guest, hungry, into the hut.

Here is guest-offering and foot-water, and this seat of grass, blameless one; and this pure barley-meal gained by observance, lord.
mahabharata:14:93.16	Accept it, good fortune to you. The brahmin ate a kudava of barley-meal, O king of kings, and was not satisfied.
The gleaner, seeing that brahmin seized by hunger, wondered how to give him food so that he would be satisfied.
His wife said, O king, "Let my share be given; let this best of brahmins go, satisfied, as he wishes."
Hearing that good woman say so, the righteous best of brahmins, knowing her seized by hunger, did not welcome that barley-meal.
Knowing her old, hungry, weary and faint, an ascetic, skin and bones, trembling, he said to his wife:

Fair one, women are to be protected and nourished even among worms, insects and beasts; you should not speak so.
mahabharata:14:93.22	A man cherished by a woman, nourished and protected, falls from blazing fame and does not gain the worlds.
So told, she said, "Dharma and wealth are equal for us two, brahmin; take this fourth part of a prastha of barley-meal; be gracious to me.
Truth, delight, dharma and heaven are won by the qualities, and for women they depend on the husband, best of brahmins; so is what is wished.
The mother's season, the father's seed, the husband the supreme god: by the husband's favour women gain delight and the fruit of sons.
By protecting me you are my husband, by supporting me my master, by giving me a son my boon-giver; therefore accept my barley-meal.
You are overtaken by old age, aged, hungry, very weak, wearied by fasting, as I am thin."
So told, he took the barley-meal and said these words: "Brahmin, accept again this barley-meal, good one."
Taking it, the brahmin ate and was not satisfied; seeing him, the gleaner became anxious.
[Son] "Take this barley-meal and give it to the brahmin, best one; I think that is well done, therefore I do this.
You are to be protected by me with all efforts, best of brahmins; this is what the good wish: the support of an aged father.
This is ordained as the purpose of a son: protection in old age; this tradition, brahmin sage, is famed in the three worlds.
You can practise austerity simply by sustaining life; for life is the highest dharma standing in the bodies of the embodied."
[Father] "Even if you reach a thousand years you are still a child to me; having begotten a son, a father is fulfilled.
Hunger is strong in children, I know this, lord; I, old, shall bear it; be strong, my son.
Hunger does not trouble me with my worn age, son; long austerity has been practised and I have no fear of death."
[Son] "I am your offspring, a son; the word son is famed from protecting; the self is held to be the son; therefore protect yourself here by yourself."
[Father] "You are like me in form, conduct and self-control, and have been tested in many ways; so I take your barley-meal."
Having said this, the best of the twice-born, pleased in soul, took that barley-meal and, as if laughing, gave it to the brahmin.
Having eaten that barley-meal too, he was still not satisfied, and the best of brahmins, the gleaner, was ashamed.
Then the good daughter-in-law, standing there, wishing to please the brahmin, took the barley-meal and said to her father-in-law, glad:

Brahmin, my offspring will come from your offspring; take this barley-meal and give it to the guest for me.
mahabharata:14:93.43	By the continuation of your line the imperishable worlds are mine; by the grandson one gains them, going where one does not grieve.
mahabharata:14:93.44	As dharma and its like are a triad, and the fire a triad, so likewise the triad of sons and grandsons in heaven is imperishable.
mahabharata:14:93.45	We have heard that a son saves the ancestors by protecting, and with sons and grandsons one surely gains good worlds.
[Father-in-law] "Seeing you, of good vows and conduct, with limbs withered by wind and sun, discoloured, thin, and your mind troubled by hunger,
how shall I take barley-meal, becoming a destroyer of dharma? Fortunate one of fair conduct, you should not speak so.
How shall I see you, who keep a vow at the sixth time, endowed with conduct and purity, in hard livelihood and without food?
You are young, hungry and a woman, and are always to be protected by me; wearied by fasting, you are the delight of kinsmen."
[Daughter-in-law] "You are my teacher's teacher, for you are the god of gods, the god above gods; therefore, lord, take my barley-meal.
Body, life and dharma exist for service to the teacher; by your grace, brahmin, I shall gain the worlds I desire.
You should take the barley-meal either thinking 'she is to be looked after', or from firm devotion, or 'she is to be cared for by me'."
[Father-in-law] "By this constant good conduct you shine, good one, you who, endowed with the vow of dharma, regard service to your elder.
So I shall take the barley-meal; you do not deserve deception; reckoning it, fortunate one, you are best of those who uphold dharma."
Having said this, he took the barley-meal and gave it to the brahmin, and the brahmin was satisfied with that good great soul.
Pleased in soul, Dharma in human form, eloquent, said to the best of brahmins these words:

I am pleased, best of brahmins, with your pure gift, justly gained and given with effort as you were able.
mahabharata:14:93.58	Ah, your gift is proclaimed in heaven by those who dwell in heaven; look at the shower of flowers fallen from the sky to the earth.
mahabharata:14:93.59	Divine sages, gods, gandharvas and the gods' leaders stand praising, and the gods' messengers, amazed by your gift.
mahabharata:14:93.60	Brahmin sages in cars, and those gone to Brahma's world, long to see you; go to heaven, best of brahmins.
mahabharata:14:93.61	All the ancestors gone to the world of the ancestors have been saved by you, and many yet to come, for many yugas.
mahabharata:14:93.62	By celibacy, sacrifice, gift and austerity, and by dharma without deceit, go therefore to heaven, brahmin.
mahabharata:14:93.63	Because you practise austerity with supreme faith, of good vows, the gods are pleased with you, best of brahmins.
mahabharata:14:93.64	Because you gave up all this with a pure mind in a time of hardship, heaven has been won by your deed.
mahabharata:14:93.65	Hunger destroys wisdom and removes right understanding; one whose knowledge is seized by hunger gives up steadfastness.
mahabharata:14:93.66	One who conquers hunger surely conquers heaven; when there is delight in giving, dharma does not decline.
mahabharata:14:93.67	Not regarding love for son and love for wife, knowing dharma as the teacher, you did not count thirst.
mahabharata:14:93.68	The gaining of goods by men is subtle, giving to a worthy one is higher than that, time is higher than giving, and faith higher than that.
mahabharata:14:93.69	The door of heaven is very subtle and not seen by men through delusion; it is barred by greed, its seed is greed, guarded by passion, hard to approach.
mahabharata:14:93.70	Men who have conquered anger and the senses see it: brahmins joined with austerity, who give as they are able.
mahabharata:14:93.71	One who can give a thousand, a hundred, or a hundred who gives ten, or even who gives water as he can, are all held to have equal fruit.
mahabharata:14:93.72	King Rantideva, owning nothing, gave water with a pure mind, brahmin, and so went to the back of heaven.
mahabharata:14:93.73	Dharma is not pleased, dear one, by great gifts of great fruit, as it is by subtle gifts justly won and purified by faith.
mahabharata:14:93.74	King Nriga gave thousands of cows to brahmins, but giving one that belonged to another, he went to hell.
mahabharata:14:93.75	By giving his own flesh, King Shibi Aushinara, of good vows, reached the worlds of the righteous and rejoices in heaven.
mahabharata:14:93.76	Merit of men does not lie in wealth; it is won by the good through their own strength, not by various sacrifices justly gathered, brahmin.
mahabharata:14:93.77	Anger destroys the fruit of giving, greed prevents going to heaven; one of just livelihood who knows giving gains heaven by austerity.
mahabharata:14:93.78	Not by many Rajasuyas performed with great fees, nor by many Ashvamedhas, is this equal fruit gained by you.
mahabharata:14:93.79	By a prastha of barley-meal you have won Brahma's world, blameless one; go, brahmin, to Brahma's stainless abode as you wish.
mahabharata:14:93.80	A divine car has come for all of you, best of brahmins; mount as you wish. I am Dharma, brahmin; look at me.
mahabharata:14:93.81	Your body has been purified by you, and your fame is firm in the world; go to heaven with your wife, son and daughter-in-law.
Thus addressed by Dharma, the brahmin, mounting the car, went to heaven with his wife, son and daughter-in-law.
When that brahmin had gone to heaven with son and daughter-in-law, and the wife, the fourth, the knower of dharma, then I came out of my hole.
Then, by the smell of barley-meal, the wetness of water, the trampling of divine flowers, and the bits of that good man's gifts, my head was turned to gold by that brahmin's austerity.
By his truthful resolve and subtle gift, brahmins, half my body was made golden; see this great thing by the wise man's austerity.
How may my other side become so? I wonder, brahmins; I go glad again and again to ascetic forests and sacrifices.
But hearing of this sacrifice of the wise Kuru king, I came with great hope, and I was not made golden.
Then I said those words, laughing, best of brahmins: "This sacrifice is not equal to the prastha of barley-meal in any way."
For by the grains of that prastha of barley-meal I was turned golden; this great sacrifice is not, to my mind, like those."
[Vaishampayana] Having said this to all the best of brahmins at the sacrifice, the mongoose disappeared, O king, and the brahmins went home.
All this has been told to you by me, scourge of enemy cities, the marvel that occurred at that great horse sacrifice.
You should not be amazed at the sacrifice, king, in any way; thousands of crores of sages have gone to heaven by austerities.
Non-malice toward all beings, contentment, conduct, uprightness, austerity, self-control, truth and giving are held equal.
[Janamejaya] "Therefore there is nothing here equal to the fruits of sacrifices; so my mind holds, and without doubt.
Many kings, best of brahmins, having sacrificed, gained supreme fame here and went from here to heaven after death.
The thousand-eyed lord of the gods, of great radiance, gained the whole kingship of the gods by sacrifices with great fees.
King Yudhishthira, with Bhima and Arjuna in front, was equal to the king of the gods in prosperity and valour.
Then why did that mongoose censure the great horse sacrifice of that great-souled king?"
[Vaishampayana] "Hear from me, king, the best rule of sacrifice and its fruit, as I tell it truly, O Bharata.
Long ago, when Shakra was sacrificing, all the great sages said, while the priests were busy and the sacrificial rite spread out,
while the fire was being offered into, the oblation endowed with many qualities, the gods being called and the great sages standing,
when at the time of slaughter the animals were seized, the great sages, great king, were filled with pity.
Then, seeing the animals pitiful, those ascetic sages came to Shakra and said: "This is not the good rule of sacrifice.
This is your ignorance, who wish for great dharma; animal hosts are not seen in the rule of sacrifice, Purandara.
This undertaking of yours, lord, destroys dharma; this is not dharma done as dharma, and harm is not called dharma.
Let them perform your sacrifice by tradition if you wish; by a sacrifice seen in the rule, great dharma will be yours.
Sacrifice with seeds, thousand-eyed one, kept for three years; this is great dharma, Shakra, found by reflection."
But Shatakratu, under the sway of pride and delusion, did not accept that word spoken by the sages who saw the truth.
A great dispute arose among those great sages, Shakra: whether one should sacrifice with moving or with immovable things, O Bharata.
Wearied by the dispute, those sages who saw truth, having agreed with Shakra, asked King Vasu.
Greatly fortunate one, how is the tradition held for sacrifices, king: should one sacrifice with pure animals or with seeds and goats?
Hearing their words, not weighing strength and weakness, the king said, "One should sacrifice with whatever is brought."
Having said this, the king, lord of the Chedis, entered the underworld, having spoken falsely here, king.
Whoever, unlearned, sacrifices with wealth unjustly gained, wishing dharma, does not gain the fruit of dharma.
And a sinful man, a hypocrite of dharma, who gives gifts to brahmins to create trust in the world,
a brahmin who by sinful acts gains wealth, unrestrained, joined with passion and delusion, gains a foul end.
Gifts given by him, sinful and of ruined mind, even vast ones, are destroyed without reaching goodness.
For him engaged in unrighteousness, a harmer, evil-souled, there is no fame from giving, here or hereafter, the ill-minded.
Even with a mind set on hoarding, fallen under greed and delusion, sinful in mind, he alarms beings with harm.
One who, having thus gained wealth, sacrifices and gives out of greed, does not succeed by that act, because of the wrong tradition.
Ascetics, by giving gleanings, roots, fruits, vegetables and a vessel of water according to their means, righteous men go to heaven.
This is great dharma: renunciation, giving, compassion for beings, celibacy, truth, mercy, steadfastness and patience; this is the eternal root of eternal dharma.
It is heard that of old brahmins and kings like Vishvamitra, Vishvamitra and Asita, King Janaka, Kakshasena, Arshtishena and King Sindhudvipa,
these and many other kings gained supreme perfection, by truth and gifts justly gained, ascetics.
Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras who rely on austerity, purified by the fire of giving and dharma, go to heaven, O Bharata."
[Janamejaya] "So what the gleaner did, the great fruit of giving barley-meal, has been told to me, brahmin; this is true without doubt.
How then would the highest certainty be among all sacrifices? You should tell me that in full, best of brahmins."
[Vaishampayana] "On this too they cite an ancient tale, scourge of foes: what happened long ago at Agastya's sacrifice, as I have it.
Long ago the greatly radiant Agastya entered a twelve-year consecration, O great king, devoted to the good of all beings.
At that great soul's sacrifice, priests like fire were there: those living on roots, those without food, those who pound with stone, drinkers of sunbeams,
parighrishtikas, vaikhasikas, and those who wash clean; ascetics and mendicants too were present.
All were direct in dharma, conquerors of anger and senses, established in self-control, free of hypocrisy and delusion.
Standing always in pure conduct and unburdened by the senses, those great sages enjoyed and attended that sacrifice.
While such a great sacrifice of Agastya was going on, the thousand-eyed one did not rain then, best of the Bharatas.
Then in a pause of the rite, O king, this tale arose among the sages of cultivated souls about the great soul Agastya.
'Agastya, the sacrificer, gives food without malice; but the rain-cloud does not rain; how will there be food?
This great sacrifice of the sage, brahmins, lasts twelve years, and the god will not rain for these twelve years.
Considering this, you should show favour to this wise great sage Agastya of great austerity.'
Thus addressed, the mighty Agastya, eloquent, appeasing the sages with bowed head, said these words:
'If Vasava does not rain for twelve years, I shall perform the sacrifice by thought; this is the eternal rule.
If Vasava does not rain for twelve years, I shall bring other sacrifices of strict vows by exertion.
This seed-sacrifice of mine has been accumulated over many years; I shall perform it with seeds made; there will be no obstacle in it.
This sacrifice of mine cannot in any way be made in vain; either the god will rain here or there will be no god.
Or Indra may make a request, not from desire; I myself shall become Indra and give life to the people.
Whatever one is made of by food, so he will be; and I shall make a distinction again and again.
Let gold come here today and whatever other rare wealth there is in the three worlds; let it come here itself.
Let the divine hosts of apsarases, with gandharvas and kinnaras, and Vishvavasu and others, ever attend you.
Whatever wealth there is from the northern Kurus, let it all come here to my sacrifice itself; heaven, the dwellers of heaven and dharma, let them come themselves.'
When this was said, all this came to the wise one; then those sages, seeing that sage's power of austerity, amazed, said these words, full of meaning:
'We are pleased by your word; we do not wish to waste austerity; we are satisfied with our own sacrifices and wish justly.
Sacrifices, consecrations, oblations and whatever else we seek, let that be by our own sacrifices; we seek nothing from elsewhere.
We who gain our food justly, devoted to our own work, seek the Vedas justly through celibacy.
We have gone out of our houses justly in later life, and shall practise austerity through the doors seen in dharma by rule.
Your understanding, free of harm, is right; so you should always speak of non-harm in sacrifices, lord.
Then we shall be pleased, best of the twice-born; dismissed at the end, we shall go from this sacrifice.'
While they were speaking so, the king of the gods, Purandara, of great radiance, seeing his power of austerity, rained.
Before the sacrifice had been completed, Mahendra of immeasurable valour, Janamejaya, became a plentiful rainer.
And the lord of the thirty gods, royal sage, himself came, putting Brihaspati first, and appeased Agastya.
Then at the completion of the sacrifice Agastya, greatly pleased, honouring them by rule, dismissed those great sages."
[Vaishampayana] "This was not asked of me before nor said by us; hear who that mongoose was and how his speech came to be human.
Jamadagni long ago planned a shraddha; the sacrificial cow came to him, and he himself milked her.
He placed that milk in a new, firm, clean vessel, and Anger, in his own form, overturned the pot.
Wishing to test that best of sages, thinking 'What will he do when offended?', the ill-minded one assaulted that milk.
Knowing him as Anger, the sage did not grow angry at him; then Anger, standing embodied with folded hands, said this:
'I am conquered, best of the Bhrigus; the Bhrigus are said to be very wrathful, but this is a false saying in the world, since I am conquered by you.
I am standing in you, forgiving great soul; I fear your austerity, good one; be gracious to me, lord.'
[Jamadagni] 'I have seen you directly, Anger; go free of fever. You have done me no wrong today, and I have no anger.'"

Having insulted the son of Dharma with that prastha of barley-meal, Anger was freed from the curse; for Yudhishthira was Dharma.
mahabharata:14:96.15	So it happened then at that great soul's sacrifice, and as we watched, the mongoose vanished there.
At times of recreation and meals, and in garlands, beds and seats, your women should be well guarded, supervised by aged trusted ones, virtuous, high-born and learned, Yudhishthira.
You should also make ministers of brahmins skilled in learning, humble, well born, skilled in dharma and wealth, and upright.
You should take counsel with them, not too much with many, nor with them all together, on any pretext.
You should take counsel in a well-covered council house or on a high place, in a forest without bushes, and never at night.
Monkeys, birds, those who imitate men, the dull and the lame should all be excluded from the council house.
The faults that come to kings from leaking of counsel cannot be remedied in any way, I think.
You should tell the faults of leaking counsel in the circle of ministers, and the merits of secrecy, again and again, scourge of foes.
You should act so that the purity and impurity of townspeople and country people are known to you, scourge of foes.
Knowing the measure, the officers should impose punishment on those to be punished, rightly, Yudhishthira.
Those fond of taking, violators of others' wives, chiefly given to harsh punishment, and liars,
revilers, the greedy, killers, those fond of violence, breakers of assembly recreation and defilers of the classes should be fined in gold or put to death, according to place and time.
In the morning you should see those who do the work of expenditure; after that you should attend to adornment and food.
Then you should see the warriors, always gladdening them; there should always be inspection by you of messengers and spies.
In the last watch of the night you should decide what is to be done, and your recreation should be at midnight and at midday.
And the time is surely at hand for the king's passing; know that the time has come, best of those who know time.
This holy, supremely purifying account was told, brahmin, by the sage Krishna, ever truthful.
